items.paragraph: Advocates of rewilding sometimes speak as though removing fences and reintroducing a few large animals will return a landscape to the condition it was in before human interference. items.paragraph: It is widely believed that a teacher's expectations can shape how well pupils perform: tell a teacher that certain children are about to blossom, and they will. There is evidence that expectations matter, since teachers who expect more of a pupil may give that pupil more attention, more time to answer questions and more demanding work. But the effects found in careful studies are usually modest, and they tend to be larger for younger children and for pupils whom the teacher does not yet know well. Expectations, in other words, are one influence among many, not a force that can by itself transform a child's results.

items.paragraph: Cities tend to think about their evenings in one of two ways. Some treat the hours after dark as a problem to be contained, a time of noise, drinking and disorder to be managed with closing times and police patrols. Others treat them as an opportunity, encouraging late markets, theatres and restaurants that bring life and employment to streets otherwise deserted after the offices close. Each view sees something real; the first notices the residents kept awake, the second the workers and visitors who depend on the night. A city that adopts only one tends to get its worst version: enforcement alone empties the streets and makes them less safe, while promotion alone pushes disorder onto the people who live nearby.
